summary.text: A stars-and-bars bound gives only $O((\log N)^B)$ integers below $N$ with digit sum at most any fixed $B$, so these exceptional sets have density zero. Using the last one or two digits, every occurrence of a value other than $8$ is assigned either to such a bounded-digit-sum set or to numbers ending in $99$, giving limsup at most $1/100$; conversely, numbers $10t+9$ with $t$ not ending in $9$ and with digit sum at least $8$ yield enough occurrences along $N=100K$ to give limsup at least $1/100$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S(n)=\text{the sum of the decimal digits of }n,
\qquad
a(n)=S(n)\bmod S(n+1).
\]
For \(N,m\in\mathbb N\), write
\[
A_m(N)=\#\{0\le n<N:a(n)=m\}.
\]
We prove that for every \(m\),
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_m(N)}N
\le
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_8(N)}N.
\]
(The value assigned to the quotient at \(N=0\) is immaterial.)

We begin with the elementary decimal-digit identities that drive the proof.
Every nonnegative integer can be written uniquely as
\[
n=10q+d,\qquad q=\left\lfloor\frac n{10}\right\rfloor,
\quad d=n\bmod 10,\quad 0\le d\le 9,
\]
and consequently
\[
S(n)=S(q)+d. \tag{1}
\]
If \(d\le 8\), adding one causes no carry, so
\[
S(n+1)=S(q)+d+1.
\]
The numerator \(S(q)+d\) is then smaller than the modulus \(S(q)+d+1\), and hence
\[
a(n)=S(q)+d \qquad(d\le 8). \tag{2}
\]

There is a second important carry calculation. Suppose that \(d=9\), that the last digit of \(q\) is not \(9\), and that \(S(q)\ge 8\). Then
\[
n=10q+9,\qquad n+1=10(q+1),
\]
and the hypothesis on the last digit of \(q\) means that adding one to \(q\) causes no carry. Thus
\[
S(n)=S(q)+9,
\qquad
S(n+1)=S(q+1)=S(q)+1.
\]
Since
\[
S(q)+9=(S(q)+1)+8
\]
and \(8<S(q)+1\), division by \(S(q)+1\) leaves remainder \(8\). Therefore
\[
a(10q+9)=8
\quad\text{if }q\bmod 10\ne9\text{ and }S(q)\ge8. \tag{3}
\]

We next prove that, for each fixed bound \(B\), integers with digit sum at most \(B\) have asymptotic density zero. Define
\[
c(N,s)=\#\{0\le t<N:S(t)=s\},
\qquad
C_B(N)=\#\{0\le t<N:S(t)\le B\}.
\]
Clearly
\[
C_B(N)=\sum_{s=0}^B c(N,s). \tag{4}
\]

We claim that for all \(D,s\ge0\),
\[
c(10^D,s)\le {D+s\choose s}. \tag{5}
\]
We prove this by induction on \(D\). For \(D=0\), the interval \([0,10^0)\) contains only \(0\), whose digit sum is \(0\), so the assertion is immediate.

For the induction step, consider the map
\[
t\longmapsto \left\lfloor\frac t{10}\right\rfloor
\]
on the set of \(t<10^{D+1}\) having \(S(t)=s\). If \(t=10q+d\), equation (1) gives
\[
S(q)=s-d\le s,
\]
so the image lies among the \(q<10^D\) with digit sum at most \(s\). Moreover, this map is injective on the fixed level set \(S(t)=s\): if \(q\) is known, then the final digit is forced to be
\[
d=s-S(q),
\]
so \(t=10q+d\) is determined. It follows that
\[
c(10^{D+1},s)\le \sum_{b=0}^s c(10^D,b).
\]
Using the induction hypothesis,
\[
c(10^{D+1},s)
 \le \sum_{b=0}^s {D+b\choose b}
 = {D+s+1\choose s},
\]
where the final equality is the hockey-stick identity. This is exactly (5) with \(D+1\) in place of \(D\), completing the induction.

For an arbitrary \(N\), let \(L=\lfloor\log_{10}N\rfloor\), with the usual harmless convention at \(N=0\). For positive \(N\),
\[
10^L\le N<10^{L+1}.
\]
Monotonicity in the endpoint and (5) therefore give
\[
c(N,s)\le c(10^{L+1},s)
\le {L+1+s\choose s}. \tag{6}
\]
For \(0\le s\le B\), we may use the elementary estimate \({x\choose s}\le x^s\) and enlarge both the base and exponent to obtain
\[
{L+1+s\choose s}
\le (L+1+B)^B.
\]
Summing (6) over \(s=0,\ldots,B\) yields
\[
C_B(N)\le (B+1)(L+1+B)^B. \tag{7}
\]
Since \(N\ge10^L\),
\[
0\le \frac{C_B(N)}N
\le \frac{(B+1)(L+1+B)^B}{10^L}. \tag{8}
\]
As \(N\to\infty\), also \(L\to\infty\). For fixed \(B\), the expression on the right tends to zero because an exponential dominates a fixed-degree polynomial. For completeness, \((L+1+B)^B\le 2^B L^B\) once \(L\ge B+1\), and \(L^B/10^L\to0\), as is seen, for example, by taking the ratio of consecutive terms, which tends to \(1/10<1\). Thus (8) proves
\[
\frac{C_B(N)}N\longrightarrow0
\qquad\text{for every fixed }B. \tag{9}
\]

We now upper-bound occurrences of any value other than \(8\). Fix \(m\ne8\), and consider an \(n<N\) with \(a(n)=m\). Put \(q=\lfloor n/10\rfloor\) and \(d=n\bmod10\). There are three exhaustive cases.

First, suppose \(d\le8\). By (2),
\[
m=S(q)+d,
\]
so in particular \(S(q)\le m\). The map \(n\mapsto q\) is injective on the set of such \(n\) with \(a(n)=m\): once \(q\) is fixed, the equality above forces \(d=m-S(q)\), and hence forces \(n=10q+d\). Also \(q<N\). Therefore the number of integers in this first case is at most
\[
C_m(N). \tag{10}
\]

Second, suppose \(d=9\) but \(q\bmod10\ne9\). If \(S(q)\ge8\), equation (3) would give \(a(n)=8\), contrary to \(a(n)=m\ne8\). Hence \(S(q)\le7\). Again \(n\mapsto q\) is injective, now simply because \(n=10q+9\). Thus the number in this second case is at most
\[
C_7(N). \tag{11}
\]

Third, suppose \(d=9\) and \(q\bmod10=9\). These two conditions say exactly that the last two decimal digits of \(n\) are \(99\), or
\[
n\equiv99\pmod {100}. \tag{12}
\]
Among the integers below \(N\), the number satisfying (12) is at most
\[
\left\lfloor\frac N{100}\right\rfloor+1. \tag{13}
\]
Indeed, division by \(100\) injects this congruence class below \(N\) into an initial interval of that size.

Combining the three cases gives
\[
A_m(N)
\le C_m(N)+C_7(N)+\left\lfloor\frac N{100}\right\rfloor+1. \tag{14}
\]
After division by \(N\), (9) and (13) show that the right-hand side tends to \(1/100\). Consequently,
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_m(N)}N\le\frac1{100}
\qquad(m\ne8). \tag{15}
\]
More explicitly, the first two terms in (14), divided by \(N\), tend to zero, while
\[
\frac{N/100+1}{N}=\frac1{100}+\frac1N\longrightarrow\frac1{100};
\]
monotonicity of limsup then gives (15).

It remains to obtain a matching lower bound for the limsup frequency of \(8\). For a positive integer \(K\), consider the set
\[
G_K=\{0\le t<10K:t\bmod10\ne9\text{ and }S(t)\ge8\}.
\]
For every \(t\in G_K\), set
\[
n=10t+9.
\]
Then \(n<100K\), and (3) shows that \(a(n)=8\). The map \(t\mapsto10t+9\) is injective, so
\[
|G_K|\le A_8(100K). \tag{16}
\]

We estimate \(|G_K|\) from below. Every \(t<10K\) which is not in \(G_K\) either ends in \(9\), or has \(S(t)\le7\). Hence
\[
10K\le |G_K|
 +\#\{0\le t<10K:t\equiv9\pmod {10}\}
 +C_7(10K). \tag{17}
\]
The middle cardinality is at most
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{10K}{10}\right\rfloor+1=K+1. \tag{18}
\]
By (9),
\[
\frac{C_7(N)}N\to0.
\]
In particular, for all sufficiently large \(N\), \(C_7(N)\le N/10\). Applying this on the subsequence \(N=10K\), we find that for all sufficiently large \(K\),
\[
C_7(10K)\le K. \tag{19}
\]
For such a \(K\), equations (17)–(19) imply
\[
10K\le |G_K|+(K+1)+K,
\]
and therefore
\[
|G_K|\ge8K-1.
\]
In particular, since we may take \(K\ge1\),
\[
|G_K|\ge K. \tag{20}
\]
Together with (16), this gives, for every sufficiently large \(K\),
\[
A_8(100K)\ge K.
\]
Thus
\[
\frac{A_8(100K)}{100K}\ge\frac1{100} \tag{21}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(K\). The indices \(100K\) are unbounded, so (21) holds at arbitrarily large cutoffs \(N\). Since every frequency \(A_8(N)/N\) lies between \(0\) and \(1\), the standard characterization of limsup as the eventual supremum now gives
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_8(N)}N\ge\frac1{100}. \tag{22}
\]
Indeed, every tail contains some index \(N=100K\) satisfying (21), so the supremum over every tail is at least \(1/100\), and taking the limit of these tail suprema proves (22).

Finally, let \(m\in\mathbb N\). If \(m=8\), the desired comparison is equality. If \(m\ne8\), combine (15) and (22):
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_m(N)}N
\le\frac1{100}
\le\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_8(N)}N.
\]
Therefore the limsup asymptotic frequency of the value \(8\) is at least that of every other value, as claimed.
